method: symmetric four-world authoring, post-hoc seeded key selection

worlds.keyAct: relaying a completed dispatch to a third party
worlds.line: Your transcript went out in yesterday's mail.
worlds.reply: Great, I'll tell the program to watch for it this week.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The clerk reports that the document has already been sent, which closes the request. The reply that tells the program to watch for it treats the matter as finished and passes the news on to the party waiting for it. The reply asking which office placed a hold invents an obstacle this line rules out; the reply brushing off the delay and naming a day to check back treats a completed request as still pending; and the reply owning a mistake and refilling a form assumes a paperwork error that was never mentioned.

kills.1: The line says the transcript "went out in yesterday's mail", so nothing is blocking it and there is no office to go and ask about a hold.
kills.2: Since it already "went out in yesterday's mail", there is nothing left in a queue and no reason to check back about it.
kills.3: The transcript "went out" as requested, so no form was wrong and there is nothing to fill in again.

worlds.keyAct: asking where to go to clear an obstacle
worlds.line: We can't process it — there's a hold on your account.
worlds.reply: Which office put the hold on? I'll go clear it.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The clerk reports a block that the student, not the office, has to remove. The reply that asks where the block came from and promises to go and clear it is what a cooperative person does when told an obstacle exists. The reply telling the program to expect the transcript would be false, since nothing was sent; the reply brushing off the delay and naming a day to check back assumes waiting will help when the student must act; and the reply about refilling a form assumes the wrong problem.

kills.0: The line says "there's a hold on your account" and that the office "can't process it", so nothing has been sent and nobody can be told to expect it.
kills.2: Waiting changes nothing here: the clerk says "We can't process it" until the student removes the block.
kills.3: The obstacle named is "a hold on your account", not a form filled in wrongly.

worlds.keyAct: committing to stop chasing and wait
worlds.line: It's still sitting in the queue behind the summer backlog.
worlds.reply: No rush then — I'll check back on Friday.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The clerk reports an ordinary delay with nothing wrong and nothing for the student to do. The reply that shrugs off the delay and names a later day to check back accepts the wait without pressing, which is the cooperative response to a queue. The reply telling the program to expect the transcript would be premature; the reply hunting for an office that placed a hold assumes a block that was not mentioned; and the reply owning a filing mistake assumes an error the clerk did not report.

kills.0: It is "still sitting in the queue", so nothing has left the office and nobody can be told to watch for it.
kills.1: Nothing is blocked — the delay is only that it sits "behind the summer backlog".
kills.3: The request is intact and merely "still sitting in the queue", so no form needs redoing.

worlds.keyAct: accepting the error and redoing the paperwork
worlds.line: You filled in the graduate form, not the undergraduate one.
worlds.reply: That's my mistake, let me fill in the right one.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The clerk corrects which form was used, so the request cannot go forward as submitted. The reply that owns the error and starts the correct form is the natural repair. The reply telling the program to expect the transcript assumes a dispatch that has not happened; the reply asking which office placed a hold names a problem the clerk did not describe; and the reply brushing off the delay and naming a day to check back treats a rejected form as if it were queued.

kills.0: The student "filled in the graduate form", which was the wrong one, so nothing has been mailed.
kills.1: There is no account problem here — the trouble is only that the form was "not the undergraduate one".
kills.2: Nothing is waiting in line; the clerk says the student "filled in the graduate form" by mistake.

worlds.keyAct: expressing relief and disclosing the cost carried
worlds.line: Your reimbursement cleared — it'll show up on next payroll.
worlds.reply: That's a relief; I'd been carrying it on my card.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The staff member reports that the claim has been approved and paid. The reply expressing relief and mentioning the card that had been carrying the cost fits a payment finally coming through. The reply asking whether scans are acceptable answers a request for documents that was never made; the reply promising to walk the form to another office assumes it was misdirected; and the reply about pulling receipts and resubmitting assumes a refusal that did not occur.

kills.1: The line says "Your reimbursement cleared", so no documents are outstanding and there is nothing to ask about submitting.
kills.2: "Your reimbursement cleared" at this desk, so the claim is settled here and there is nothing to carry to another office.
kills.3: Since "Your reimbursement cleared", no part of the claim was refused and nothing needs resubmitting.

worlds.keyAct: clarifying the acceptable format before complying
worlds.line: Could you bring in the original boarding passes this week?
worlds.reply: Sure — do scans work, or does it have to be paper?
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The staff member asks the student to supply supporting documents. The reply that agrees and checks what form the documents may take is exactly the cooperative next move when told to bring something in. The reply expressing relief about a card assumes money has arrived; the reply about walking a form to another office assumes it was misdirected; and the reply pulling receipts to resubmit assumes something was refused.

kills.0: This is a request to "bring in the original boarding passes", not a payment notice, so nothing has cleared yet.
kills.2: The desk wants documents brought here — "bring in the original boarding passes" — so nothing is being sent elsewhere.
kills.3: Nothing was refused; the office asks the student to add "the original boarding passes", not to remove anything.

worlds.keyAct: committing to redirect the paperwork
worlds.line: The travel form goes to the dean's office, not us.
worlds.reply: I'll walk it over there this afternoon, then.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The staff member corrects where the paperwork belongs. The reply that undertakes to carry it to the right place this afternoon is the obvious repair when told you are at the wrong counter. The reply expressing relief about money assumes a payment that has not been made; the reply asking whether scans are acceptable answers a request for documents that was not made; and the reply pulling receipts to resubmit assumes a decision that has not been taken.

kills.0: Nothing has been decided about money; the line only says the form "goes to the dean's office".
kills.1: No documents were asked for — the point is where the form "goes to the dean's office".
kills.3: Nothing was denied; the form simply "goes to the dean's office" instead of here.

worlds.keyAct: conceding the ruling and revising the claim
worlds.line: We're not covering meals for a single-day trip.
worlds.reply: Fair enough — I'll pull those receipts and resubmit.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The staff member rules part of the claim ineligible. The reply that accepts the ruling and undertakes to strip out the disallowed items and submit again is the cooperative way to salvage the rest. The reply expressing relief about money assumes a payment; the reply asking whether scans are acceptable assumes a document request; and the reply about carrying the form elsewhere assumes it was at the wrong desk rather than partly refused.

kills.0: "We're not covering meals" is a refusal, not a payment, so there is no relief to express.
kills.1: No documents were requested; the issue is that the office is "not covering meals".
kills.2: This office is the one deciding — "We're not covering meals" — so the form is in the right place.

worlds.keyAct: redirecting effort to the next piece of work
worlds.line: Chapter three works now — I'd send it to your committee.
worlds.reply: Then I'll spend this week on the conclusion instead.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The supervisor releases the chapter and advises sending it on. The reply that moves the week's work to a later part of the thesis follows from a chapter that no longer needs attention. The reply asking where the argument breaks down contradicts a positive verdict; the reply accepting a Thursday working session takes up an offer that was not made; and the reply about a stale file assumes the supervisor read the wrong draft.

kills.1: The supervisor says "Chapter three works now", so there is no breakdown to point to.
kills.2: No meeting was proposed; the advice is to "send it to your committee".
kills.3: The verdict is on the current chapter — it "works now" — so no wrong version was read.

worlds.keyAct: asking for a diagnosis of the failure
worlds.line: The core argument in chapter three still doesn't hold.
worlds.reply: Where does the argument break down for you?
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The supervisor delivers a substantive negative verdict without saying where the trouble lies. Asking where it breaks down is what a student needs to know in order to repair it. The reply moving on to the conclusion abandons a chapter that has just failed; the reply accepting a working session takes up an offer that was not made; and the reply about resending the current file assumes the wrong draft was read.

kills.0: The argument "still doesn't hold", so the week belongs to this chapter, not to a later one.
kills.2: No time was offered — the supervisor only reports that the argument "doesn't hold".
kills.3: The complaint is about "The core argument" itself, not about which file was opened.

worlds.keyAct: accepting the working session and preparing for it
worlds.line: I could sit with you Thursday and work through chapter three.
worlds.reply: Thursday's good — I'll bring a printout.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The supervisor offers time to work on the chapter together. Accepting the day and undertaking to bring something to work from is the natural uptake of an offer to sit down together. The reply shifting the week to the conclusion assumes the chapter is finished; the reply asking where the argument breaks down assumes a verdict that was not given; and the reply about resending a current file assumes a mix-up that was not mentioned.

kills.0: An offer to "sit with you Thursday" is not a release of the chapter, so the week cannot move on.
kills.1: No fault was named; the supervisor only proposes to "work through chapter three" together.
kills.3: Nothing suggests the wrong draft was read — the offer is simply to "sit with you Thursday".

worlds.keyAct: explaining the mismatch and resending the right file
worlds.line: The version I read was your October draft, not the new one.
worlds.reply: That explains the notes — I'll resend the current file.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The supervisor realises the comments were made on an out-of-date draft. The reply that makes sense of the comments in that light and undertakes to send the current file is the obvious repair. The reply moving on to the conclusion assumes an approval that was not given; the reply asking where the argument breaks down treats stale comments as a verdict; and the reply accepting a Thursday session takes up an offer that was not made.

kills.0: Reading "your October draft" gives no verdict at all on the current chapter.
kills.1: The trouble is the file, which was "not the new one", rather than the argument.
kills.2: No meeting is proposed; the line is only about which "version I read".

worlds.keyAct: noting the convenience of continuity
worlds.line: Your tutor's the same one you had in the fall.
worlds.reply: Good — I won't have to explain where I got stuck.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The desk reports that the student has been matched with someone already familiar with their work. The reply noting that no back-story will need explaining follows directly from continuity with a previous tutor. The reply offering to move to a morning assumes nothing is available; the reply promising to fill in a week of availability answers a request that was not made; and the reply taking a newly opened slot assumes a fresh offer.

kills.1: The tutor is already assigned — "the same one you had" — so no time needs shifting to free something up.
kills.2: No availability was requested; the match is done with "the same one you had in the fall".
kills.3: A named tutor is already in place, "the same one you had", so there is no new opening to take.

worlds.keyAct: offering flexibility to unblock the match
worlds.line: Nobody's free for statistics in your Tuesday slot.
worlds.reply: I could move to a morning if that opens anything.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The desk reports that no tutor can be matched at the time the student asked for. Offering to move to a different part of the day is the cooperative way to give the desk something to work with. The reply about not having to explain where they got stuck assumes a familiar tutor; the reply promising to fill in availability answers a request that was not made; and the reply taking a slot assumes an opening that was just denied.

kills.0: "Nobody's free for statistics" means no tutor at all has been assigned, familiar or otherwise.
kills.2: The obstacle is not a missing form — it is that "Nobody's free for statistics".
kills.3: There is nothing to take, since "Nobody's free" at the hour in question.

worlds.keyAct: committing to supply the missing information
worlds.line: Could you fill in your availability before we match you?
worlds.reply: I'll fill my whole week in before tonight.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The desk asks for the student's schedule as a precondition for matching. Undertaking to enter a full week straight away is the direct compliance the request calls for. The reply about not having to explain where they got stuck assumes a tutor is already assigned; the reply offering to move to a morning assumes a refusal; and the reply taking a slot assumes an offer that has not been made.

kills.0: Nobody has been matched: the desk asks for availability "before we match you".
kills.1: Nothing has been refused — the desk only asks the student to "fill in your availability".
kills.3: There is no slot on the table yet; matching comes only "before we match you" is satisfied.

worlds.keyAct: accepting the offered slot
worlds.line: There's an opening with Ravi at your Tuesday time.
worlds.reply: I'll take it — Tuesdays are already clear for me.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The desk offers a specific tutor at the hour the student wanted. Accepting and confirming that the hour is free is the natural uptake. The reply about not having to explain where they got stuck assumes the tutor is a familiar one; the reply offering to move to a morning assumes the hour does not work; and the reply promising to fill in availability answers a request that was not made.

kills.0: "There's an opening with Ravi" introduces a tutor by name, not the one from a previous term.
kills.1: The hour asked for works — the opening is "at your Tuesday time" — so nothing needs moving.
kills.2: No form is needed once "There's an opening" has been offered outright.

worlds.keyAct: committing to rebook the lost session
worlds.line: Your consultant called in sick, so this hour's cancelled.
worlds.reply: I'll rebook myself for later in the week.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: Reception reports that the appointment cannot go ahead at all. Undertaking to book another time later in the week is what a student does when a session falls through. The reply asking about a building assumes a change of room rather than a cancellation; the reply about printing a sheet beforehand answers an instruction that was not given; and the reply accepting a full hour takes up an offer of time that no longer exists.

kills.1: Nothing moved anywhere — the line says "this hour's cancelled".
kills.2: No future requirement was named; the news is only that the consultant "called in sick".
kills.3: There is no session left to lengthen once "this hour's cancelled".

worlds.keyAct: checking which building is meant
worlds.line: We've moved to the annex — the main room's being painted.
worlds.reply: Is that the building behind the chapel?
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: Reception reports a temporary change of room, and the new location may not be obvious. Checking which building is meant is exactly what a student needs before walking over. The reply about rebooking assumes the session is off; the reply about printing a sheet beforehand answers an instruction that was not given; and the reply accepting a full hour takes up an offer that was not made.

kills.0: Nothing was cancelled — "We've moved to the annex" and the session still stands.
kills.2: No document was requested; the point is that "the main room's being painted".
kills.3: No extra time is on offer — only the room changed when "We've moved to the annex".

worlds.keyAct: confirming compliance and where the item comes from
worlds.line: Bring the assignment sheet next time, not just the draft.
worlds.reply: It's on the course site — I'll print it beforehand.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The consultant asks the student to bring an extra document to the following session. Saying where the document lives and undertaking to print it in advance is direct compliance with the request. The reply about rebooking assumes a cancellation; the reply asking about a building assumes a change of room; and the reply accepting a full hour takes up an offer of time that was not made.

kills.0: Nothing is cancelled; the consultant is planning what to "Bring" to the "next time" they meet.
kills.1: No room change is mentioned — the instruction is about what to bring "next time".
kills.3: Nothing longer was offered; the ask is only for "the assignment sheet".

worlds.keyAct: accepting the longer session and justifying the need
worlds.line: I can give you the full hour if you want it.
worlds.reply: Yes please — the introduction alone will take a while.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The consultant offers to extend the session to its full length. Accepting and naming the part of the draft that will absorb the time is the natural uptake of an offer of more time. The reply about rebooking assumes a cancellation; the reply asking about a building assumes a change of room; and the reply about printing a sheet beforehand answers an instruction that was not given.

kills.0: An offer of "the full hour" is the opposite of a session falling through.
kills.1: There is nowhere else to go — the offer is to work here for "the full hour".
kills.2: No materials were asked for; the offer concerns "the full hour if you want it".

worlds.keyAct: swapping the wrong music out
worlds.line: You're down for the Brahms this term, not the Schubert.
worlds.reply: I'll swap the music in my folder tonight.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The teacher corrects which piece the student is registered to perform. Undertaking to change the music carried in the folder follows from having the wrong score prepared. The reply about arranging rehearsal times assumes an accompanist has been found; the reply about getting something up to tempo answers a request to play that was not made; and the reply about sitting in on earlier juries assumes a running order was given.

kills.1: No accompanist is mentioned; the line only settles that the student is "down for the Brahms".
kills.2: Nothing was asked to be played on a date — the line assigns repertoire, "the Brahms this term".
kills.3: No running order is given by "the Brahms this term, not the Schubert".

worlds.keyAct: taking the initiative on rehearsals
worlds.line: We've found you an accompanist for the recital.
worlds.reply: I'll get rehearsal times sorted with them this week.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The teacher reports that the missing player has been found. Moving straight to arranging rehearsal times is what follows once there is someone to rehearse with. The reply about swapping music in a folder assumes a change of piece; the reply about getting something up to tempo answers a request to play that was not made; and the reply about sitting in on earlier juries assumes a running order.

kills.0: No repertoire changes here — the news is only that "We've found you an accompanist".
kills.2: Nothing is requested for a class; the line reports that "We've found you an accompanist".
kills.3: An "accompanist for the recital" says nothing about the order of juries.

worlds.keyAct: committing to have the piece ready
worlds.line: Play me the second movement at Friday's studio class.
worlds.reply: I'll have it up to tempo by then.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The teacher asks the student to perform a specific movement at an upcoming class. Undertaking to have it up to speed by that class is direct compliance. The reply about swapping music in a folder assumes a change of piece; the reply about rehearsal times assumes an accompanist has been found; and the reply about sitting in on earlier juries assumes a running order was announced.

kills.0: No wrong piece is named — the student is asked to "Play me the second movement".
kills.1: No accompanist is involved in "Friday's studio class".
kills.3: The line fixes a single task at "Friday's studio class", not a jury order.

worlds.keyAct: drawing a plan from the running order
worlds.line: Your jury's the last one on the Thursday list.
worlds.reply: Then I can sit in on the earlier ones.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The teacher reports where the student falls in the day's running order. Realising that everything else happens first, and planning to watch it, follows directly from being placed at the end. The reply about swapping music assumes a change of piece; the reply about rehearsal times assumes an accompanist; and the reply about being up to tempo answers a request to play that was not made.

kills.0: No piece is corrected — the line only places the student "last one on the Thursday list".
kills.1: Nobody is assigned to play alongside; the line concerns only "the Thursday list".
kills.2: Nothing is requested for a class; the jury is "on the Thursday list".

worlds.keyAct: proposing a workaround for the closure
worlds.line: The recording booths are down until the software's reinstalled.
worlds.reply: I'll do mine on my laptop and upload it.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The lab attendant reports that the equipment cannot be used for now. Proposing to record elsewhere and upload the file is the practical way around a closure. The reply about coming at a particular time assumes the hours are the issue; the reply about renaming files answers a filing instruction that was not given; and the reply about guessing at buttons takes up an offer of help that was not made.

kills.1: Opening times are beside the point while "The recording booths are down".
kills.2: No naming rule was given; the news is that "The recording booths are down".
kills.3: Nothing can be demonstrated on equipment that is "down until the software's reinstalled".

worlds.keyAct: deciding when to come in
worlds.line: The lab opens an hour earlier on Fridays now.
worlds.reply: That's when I'll come — afternoons are always packed.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The attendant reports a change to the lab's opening times. Choosing the newly available stretch and saying why the usual one is unattractive is a natural response to hearing about extra hours. The reply about recording on a laptop assumes the booths are unusable; the reply about renaming files answers an instruction that was not given; and the reply about guessing at buttons takes up an offer that was not made.

kills.0: Nothing is broken — the lab simply "opens an hour earlier" than before.
kills.2: No file convention appears in "opens an hour earlier on Fridays".
kills.3: No help was offered; the news is only about when the lab "opens an hour earlier".

worlds.keyAct: committing to fix past filings as well
worlds.line: Save your files under your student ID, not your name.
worlds.reply: I'll rename the ones I've already left there.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The attendant gives a filing rule for work stored in the lab. Undertaking to bring earlier files into line with the rule is thorough compliance with an instruction about naming. The reply about recording on a laptop assumes the booths are unusable; the reply about coming at a particular hour assumes the times changed; and the reply about guessing at buttons takes up an offer of help that was not made.

kills.0: Nothing stops the equipment being used — the student is told how to "Save your files".
kills.1: No hours appear in "Save your files under your student ID".
kills.3: No walkthrough is offered — only the instruction to "Save your files under your student ID".

worlds.keyAct: accepting the demonstration and admitting the gap
worlds.line: I can walk you through the pronunciation tool now.
worlds.reply: Yes — I've been guessing at half its buttons.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The attendant offers to demonstrate a piece of software. Accepting and admitting to having muddled through it is the natural uptake of an offer to be shown how something works. The reply about recording on a laptop assumes the booths are unusable; the reply about coming at a particular hour assumes the times changed; and the reply about renaming files answers a filing instruction that was not given.

kills.0: The software is usable — the offer is to "walk you through the pronunciation tool" right away.
kills.1: No schedule change is stated; the offer concerns "the pronunciation tool now".
kills.2: No filing rule is given; the offer is to "walk you through the pronunciation tool".

worlds.keyAct: passing the corrected detail on to others
worlds.line: We leave from the north gate, not the science building.
worlds.reply: I'll pass that on to the people I'm riding with.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The organiser corrects the meeting point for departure. Undertaking to tell the others travelling together is what a student does with a detail their group would otherwise get wrong. The reply about using the weekend for reading assumes the trip is off; the reply about borrowing boots answers a kit instruction that was not given; and the reply about asking a roommate takes up a spare-seat offer that was not made.

kills.1: The trip is going ahead — "We leave from the north gate" as planned.
kills.2: No kit was requested; the line only fixes where "We leave from".
kills.3: No seat is offered; the line corrects the meeting point, "not the science building".

worlds.keyAct: repurposing the freed time
worlds.line: The coach company cancelled, so the trip's off this weekend.
worlds.reply: I'll use the weekend for the reading instead.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The organiser reports that the trip will not happen. Putting the freed days to another use is the natural response to a cancellation. The reply about passing on a meeting point assumes the trip is running; the reply about borrowing boots assumes a kit instruction; and the reply about asking a roommate takes up an offer of a seat that no longer exists.

kills.0: There is no meeting point worth relaying once "the trip's off this weekend".
kills.2: No boots are needed if "the trip's off this weekend".
kills.3: No spare seat exists — "The coach company cancelled".

worlds.keyAct: flagging a gap and solving it
worlds.line: Bring boots — the site path is mud after rain.
worlds.reply: Mine are at home, so I'll borrow a pair.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The organiser tells the group what footwear the ground demands. Admitting the item is not to hand and undertaking to borrow some is direct compliance with a kit instruction. The reply about passing on a meeting point assumes a correction to the departure arrangements; the reply about using the weekend for reading assumes a cancellation; and the reply about asking a roommate takes up an offer of a seat that was not made.

kills.0: No departure point is stated; the instruction is only to "Bring boots".
kills.1: The trip is clearly on, since "the site path is mud after rain" still matters.
kills.3: Nobody is invited along; the line only says to "Bring boots" for the ground underfoot.

worlds.keyAct: accepting on someone else's behalf
worlds.line: There's a spare seat if your roommate wants to come.
worlds.reply: She'll jump at that — I'll ask her tonight.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The organiser opens a place on the trip to someone outside the class. Predicting the invited person will want it and undertaking to ask is the natural uptake of an offer made on a third party's behalf. The reply about passing on a meeting point assumes a correction that was not made; the reply about using the weekend for reading assumes a cancellation; and the reply about borrowing boots answers a kit instruction that was not given.

kills.0: No location is corrected — the line offers "a spare seat".
kills.1: The trip is plainly running, or there would be no "spare seat" to give away.
kills.2: Nothing is required to bring; the offer is only "if your roommate wants to come".

worlds.keyAct: drawing a consequence for what materials are needed
worlds.line: We're each taking whole sections instead of splitting questions.
worlds.reply: Then I'll only need the rubric for mine.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The lead TA describes how the marking is being divided. Working out that only one section's rubric is now relevant follows directly from taking whole sections rather than shared questions. The reply about starting with a colleague's marking assumes a regrade was requested; the reply about pulling scripts and writing up reasoning assumes a complaint; and the reply about forwarding a folder takes up an offer that was not made.

kills.1: Nobody's marking is being revisited; the plan is simply "taking whole sections".
kills.2: No complaint is raised by a decision to work "instead of splitting questions".
kills.3: Nothing was taken off anyone — the arrangement is "each taking whole sections".

worlds.keyAct: agreeing and proposing a way to track changes
worlds.line: Could you regrade the essays that Daniel marked first?
worlds.reply: I'll start with his; anything I change I'll flag.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The lead TA asks for a colleague's marking to be gone over again. Agreeing to begin there and to mark up any alterations is careful compliance with a regrade request. The reply about needing only one rubric assumes a division of sections; the reply about pulling scripts and writing up reasoning assumes a complaint; and the reply about forwarding a folder takes up an offer that was not made.

kills.0: This is a task, not a split of labour — the ask is to "regrade the essays".
kills.2: No appeal is mentioned; the subject is "the essays that Daniel marked".
kills.3: Work is being added rather than removed by "Could you regrade the essays".

worlds.keyAct: preparing a documented defence
worlds.line: Students are appealing the midterm curve in your section.
worlds.reply: I'll pull their scripts and write up my reasoning.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The lead TA reports that marks are being formally challenged. Retrieving the papers and setting down the reasoning behind them is what a marker does when a decision has to be defended. The reply about needing only one rubric assumes a division of sections; the reply about starting with a colleague's marking assumes a regrade request; and the reply about forwarding a folder takes up an offer that was not made.

kills.0: No allocation is described; the news is that "Students are appealing".
kills.1: Nobody asked for a colleague's marking to be redone — the issue is "the midterm curve".
kills.3: Nothing is offered; "Students are appealing the midterm curve" is a problem, not a favour.

worlds.keyAct: accepting the relief and handing the work over
worlds.line: I'll take the late submissions off you this round.
worlds.reply: That'd clear my weekend — I'll forward the folder.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The lead TA offers to absorb one pile of marking. Noting the weekend it frees and undertaking to send the material across is the natural uptake of an offer to take work away. The reply about needing only one rubric assumes a division of sections; the reply about starting with a colleague's marking assumes a regrade request; and the reply about pulling scripts and writing up reasoning assumes a complaint.

worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The organiser asks the colleague to chair the session. Reading the speaker's current work in advance is what preparing to introduce someone and field questions requires. The reply about changing signs assumes a venue correction; the reply telling the mailing list not to come assumes a cancellation; and the reply about a weight off the week treats a request for work as an offer to remove it.

kills.0: No venue is mentioned; the ask is to "introduce her and handle the questions".
kills.1: The event is on, since somebody must "introduce her" on the day.
kills.3: You are being asked to do more, not less: "Could you introduce her".

worlds.keyAct: accepting relief from the duty
worlds.line: I can chair it if you'd rather just attend.
worlds.reply: That would take a real weight off this week.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: A colleague offers to take on the chairing duty. Accepting by noting the pressure it removes is the natural uptake of an offer to absorb a task. The reply about changing signs assumes a venue correction; the reply telling the mailing list not to come assumes a cancellation; and the reply about reading a paper tonight assumes the role is still yours.

kills.0: Nothing is said about the room; the offer is to "chair it".
kills.1: The event is going ahead — the offer is to "chair it if you'd rather just attend".
kills.2: You are being relieved of the role, not given it: "if you'd rather just attend".

worlds.keyAct: moving the team on to the next deliverable
worlds.line: The sponsor signed off on your prototype yesterday.
worlds.reply: I'll move the team onto the final report.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The supervisor reports that the client has approved the build. Redirecting the team to the write-up follows from a prototype that no longer needs work. The reply proposing to reuse existing work assumes the project collapsed; the reply about arranging travel assumes the meeting place changed; and the reply about meeting minutes answers a request that was not made.

kills.1: Nothing has collapsed — the sponsor "signed off on your prototype".
kills.2: No change of venue is mentioned in "signed off on your prototype yesterday".
kills.3: No write-up is requested; the line reports that the sponsor "signed off".

worlds.keyAct: negotiating to salvage existing work
worlds.line: The sponsor's pulled out, so you'll need a new brief.
worlds.reply: Could we build on the work we've already done?
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The supervisor reports that the client has withdrawn and the project must be redefined. Asking whether the existing work can carry over is what a team wants to know when facing a fresh brief. The reply about moving to the final report assumes approval; the reply about arranging travel assumes a change of meeting place; and the reply about meeting minutes answers a request that was not made.

kills.0: There is no approved build to write up, since "you'll need a new brief".
kills.2: There is no client office to visit — "The sponsor's pulled out".
kills.3: No history of changes matters now that "you'll need a new brief".

worlds.keyAct: arranging the logistics the change creates
worlds.line: Your check-ins move to the sponsor's office from now on.
worlds.reply: I'll sort out travel for the whole team.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The supervisor reports that meetings will happen off campus from here on. Arranging how the team gets there is the practical consequence of a change of venue. The reply about moving to the final report assumes approval; the reply proposing to reuse existing work assumes the project collapsed; and the reply about meeting minutes answers a request that was not made.

kills.0: No approval is given; only the meeting place changes, "to the sponsor's office".
kills.1: The client is still involved, since "check-ins move to the sponsor's office".
kills.3: Nothing is asked to be written; the line concerns where "Your check-ins move".

worlds.keyAct: committing to reconstruct the record
worlds.line: Write up what the sponsor changed since the first brief.
worlds.reply: I'll go back through the meeting minutes.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The supervisor asks for a documented account of how the requirements shifted. Going back through the record of meetings is how such an account gets assembled. The reply about moving to the final report assumes approval; the reply proposing to reuse existing work assumes the project collapsed; and the reply about arranging travel assumes a change of meeting place.

kills.0: Nothing is approved; the student is told to "Write up what the sponsor changed".
kills.1: The client is still engaged and has been changing things "since the first brief".
kills.2: No relocation is mentioned in "Write up what the sponsor changed".
